The pump that saved you money on the crush pad is the one bruising your wine in March.

One cellar pump cannot do both jobs well. A progressive cavity rotor carries skins and heavy lees through the line without chopping them. Put finished wine through a centrifugal at full speed and you get flow, shear and dissolved oxygen in the same pass.

Rotary lobe sits between them: low shear at low rpm, reversible so you can clear a line, and cleanable in place if the fittings are sanitary.

Ask for the flow curve at your actual line size, not the headline number on the front of the brochure.

A 40-ton red harvest does not need a 40-ton tank. It needs one tank for every lot you mean to keep apart.

The most expensive sizing mistake in a cellar is buying fermentation capacity by annual volume instead of by lot. You end up blending two blocks you meant to keep apart, or filling a 10,000 L tank to a third and fighting oxygen all winter.

The working rule: about 1,000 litres of red fermenter per ton of fruit, about 700 litres of white tank per ton of fruit, then round up to the next catalogue size. Tanks run from a few hundred litres to tens of thousands.

Most of the oxidation you taste in spring was dissolved into the wine during a ten-minute transfer last autumn.

Count the places air meets wine when you fill from the top. A fitting that whistles under suction. The free fall through the open hatch. The splash into a tank full of air. The headspace that stays open until someone gets round to topping. Four, in one move.

Fill valve to valve into a purged tank and close it the same hour, and that count drops to one: the surface itself.

Most of that costs nothing but sequence. The rest is the right gaskets and a pump that will run slow.

DN50 is not 50 millimetres of wine. It is a 2-inch line, and that gap has ordered a lot of wrong gaskets.

Most of the best cellar equipment is Italian or French, so the quote arrives in DN: a nominal bore, a size designation rather than a measurement. Your cellar buys hose and clamps in inches. Somewhere between the two conventions a fitting turns up that will not seat, usually on the morning you needed to rack.

The mapping is fixed. DN25 is 1 inch, DN40 is 1.5, DN50 is 2, DN65 is 2.5, DN80 is 3, DN100 is 4. Save the card and check it before the PO, not on the loading dock.

Every cellar learns the same lesson in a different place. The fruit that sat warm on the pad because intake could not keep up. The press that ran all day and cleared less than it should have, because capacity is not cycle time. The two blocks you meant to keep apart and blended anyway, because the tank that was free was the wrong size.

That is your equipment brief for next year, and it is only accurate this week.

The reason to act on it now is the calendar. Crusher-destemmers run 8 to 12 weeks, presses 12 to 16, tanks 10 to 14, bottling lines 16 to 24 — before freight and commissioning.

Your crusher-destemmer is sized by your worst morning, not your annual tonnage.

Three blocks arrive at once, the fruit is warming on the pad, and the machine that coped fine all season becomes the bottleneck that decides your vintage.

Take your peak-day intake, divide by the hours you actually have, then buy a step up — rated throughput is measured on clean, dry, hand-picked fruit, not on a rainy pick full of MOG. Machines run from a couple of tons an hour to well over a hundred.

Six weeks out of fifty-two decide whether the year worked.

Every machine in your cellar is judged in those six weeks. The rest of the year it can be slow, awkward or oversized and nobody notices. In September it either keeps up or it costs you fruit.

Which is exactly why the three specs that matter least on a quote matter most in practice: how long it takes to build, whether parts still exist in five years, and how fast service answers the phone during harvest. A bargain that cannot be repaired in September was never a bargain.

Work backwards from your next crush date, not forwards from today.

If your fruit lands in February, this is the month the calendar stops being flexible.

Most of the world's best winery equipment is built in Italy and France, and both largely close through August. On top of the build sits freight, customs and commissioning — and the machine has to be running before the fruit arrives, not merely delivered.

Work it backwards from a February crush. A press at 12 to 16 weeks should already be on order. A bottling line at 16 to 24 weeks was ideally ordered last month. A destemmer or a tank still has a little room, but not much.

Most of our manufacturers build in Europe, and each one quotes its own build slot, so you know what still makes your vintage before you commit.

You do not need 316L everywhere. You do need it somewhere — and a bad weld cancels either grade.

304 is the food-grade workhorse and meaningfully cheaper: right for most tank bodies in a normal cellar. 316L earns its premium where chlorides and low pH live — coastal air, hard water, aggressive sanitation. The “L” is low carbon, which protects the corrosion resistance right at the welds.

Ask which surfaces are which, whether the interior welds were back-purged and passivated, and whether the material certs exist. A premium grade on a rough weld is still a rough weld.

Two wineries order the same press from the same manufacturer for the same price. One presses fruit in February. The other hires a machine.

The difference is not negotiation. It is the month on the purchase order.

Order this autumn and the build slot is booked before the European factories close for August, freight leaves with room to spare, and a customs hold is an inconvenience rather than a lost vintage. Order in December and you are queued behind the northern hemisphere's own rush, quoting freight at peak season, with no slack left anywhere in the chain.

Nobody plans to order late. It happens because the machine still feels like a next-year decision in the autumn.

The filtration sum is one line of arithmetic, and almost nobody does it before they shop.

Litres to filter, divided by the hours you will actually run. Twenty thousand litres over a ten-hour day is 2,000 L/hr minimum. Spread it over two days and 1,000 L/hr will do, if your bottling date can wait.

Then add margin, because rated throughput is measured on clean wine in a factory, not on the turbid post-ferment wine you are actually pushing. Buy a step above the number you land on.

Crossflow systems commonly run 500 to 10,000 L/hr, rated on clean wine.
